text: IW_BENCH_SHORT_01: The update improves startup reliability and keeps existing configuration files unchanged.
IW_BENCH_SHORT_02: Save your work before restarting the service, then confirm that the health check returns successfully.

IW_BENCH_MEDIUM_01: The translation adapter accepts OpenAI-compatible requests from the browser extension and forwards a carefully constructed prompt to an authenticated command-line model. It limits concurrent model executions, records a request identifier for troubleshooting, and returns the translated text through a local HTTP endpoint. Operators can adjust the batching window to trade a small amount of latency for fewer repeated prompts, but a larger queue cannot increase the underlying model throughput. When a page contains many independently translated elements, completion time depends on request arrival patterns, the number of available backend slots, command startup cost, network conditions, provider queueing, and model generation speed.

IW_BENCH_MEDIUM_02: A useful performance investigation should separate the time spent waiting for local capacity from the time spent executing the command-line client. It should also compare that direct path with the complete HTTP service path under the same model, reasoning effort, source text, and translation instructions. One observation is not enough because cloud response time naturally varies. Repeated measurements, warm-up samples, percentile summaries, timeout counts, and request identifiers provide a more reliable picture. The result should be treated as diagnostic evidence rather than proof that a particular network component or remote service caused the delay.

IW_BENCH_LONG_01: Reliable translation performance depends on several independent layers that are easy to confuse when only the final page completion time is visible. The browser extension first discovers text nodes, groups or splits them according to page structure, and submits requests as content appears. Lazy loading, scrolling, subtitles, navigation, and dynamic components can all change the arrival pattern. A page with many links may create short requests over a long period, while a static article may produce a dense burst. These two workloads can contain the same total number of characters but behave very differently at the adapter queue.

The local adapter then validates each request, constructs a prompt, and decides whether the item is eligible for micro-batching. A batching window can reduce repeated system instructions when compatible requests arrive close together. The same window also adds delay to a singleton request, and it cannot help when items use incompatible settings or arrive after the window closes. The maximum batch size is only a ceiling; it does not mean the adapter waits indefinitely for a full batch. Concurrency controls how many backend calls may execute at once, while the pending limit controls how many accepted requests may wait for batching or execution. Raising the pending limit can absorb a short burst, but it cannot create additional model capacity.

After dispatch, a command-line client must start or reuse a process, load its configuration, find authenticated credentials, establish network connections, wait for the provider, and receive generated text. A persistent transport can remove part of the repeated process startup work, but it does not remove Internet latency, provider-side queueing, rate limits, or model reasoning time. A fast interactive response also does not guarantee the same behavior under concurrent automated requests because the provider may schedule those requests differently. Token count, prompt length, cache state, model selection, and reasoning effort can influence both latency and output.

A benchmark should therefore measure more than one aggregate duration. Direct command execution provides a baseline for the combined client, network, provider, and model path. The HTTP measurement includes that path plus adapter validation, queueing, batching, serialization, and service overhead. Repeating the same marked cases allows failures and incorrect response mapping to be detected without requiring translations to be identical. Warm-up samples should be retained for diagnostics but excluded from percentile summaries because process initialization and connection setup can make the first request structurally different from later requests.

Percentiles and variability matter because averages can hide the behavior that users notice. A service may have an acceptable median while occasionally exceeding the browser extension timeout. Reporting the minimum, median, upper percentiles, maximum, timeout rate, and coefficient of variation makes that tail behavior visible. Request identifiers should be preserved so an operator can correlate a slow HTTP sample with service events for queue duration, backend execution, batch size, and process lifecycle. Even with those measurements, the report must avoid claiming that it can separate network transmission from provider queueing or model generation unless the upstream client exposes those timings directly.

The safest conclusion is evidence-based and limited in scope. If direct command calls are already slow and highly variable, the adapter is unlikely to be the only cause. If direct calls are stable but the HTTP path adds a consistent delay, the operator should inspect local queueing, batching, and service configuration. If latency rises mainly under concurrency, capacity limits or provider throttling may be involved. The benchmark should make these patterns easier to see while preserving credentials, avoiding repository modifications, bounding child processes, and warning users before consuming account quota.
